docs.title: What is Kali?
docs.text:
Kali (also called Arnis or Eskrima) is the national martial art of the Philippines. It is a weapon-based system — primarily stick and blade — that also encompasses empty-hand combat. What makes Kali unique:

  • Weapon training comes first, transferring naturally to open-hand fighting
  • Strong emphasis on flow, angles of attack, and defanging the snake (disarming)
  • Highly practical: every movement has direct application
  • Teaches you to deal with armed opponents from day one

docs.text: Section What's Inside Fundamentals Stances, grips, the 12 angles — the non-negotiable foundation Weapons Technique breakdowns for single stick, double stick, and knife Drills Solo and partner drills: sinawali, sombrada, sparring protocol Conditioning Warm-up, strength work, and recovery routines Resources Glossary, lineage, recommended reading & videos

docs.title: Today's Training Checklist
docs.text:
Use this before every session. Tap to check off as you go — resets when you close the tab.

Warm-up complete Reviewed today's target technique Solo drill — slow reps (muscle memory, not speed) Solo drill — full speed Partner drill (if applicable) Cool-down and stretching Note anything to review next session

Learning philosophy

"Slow is smooth. Smooth is fast." — Focus on form before speed. A sloppy fast strike is less effective than a precise slow one. Film yourself when possible.

Safety first

Always gear up for partner work. Rattan sticks, padded gloves, and eye protection are non-negotiable during live sparring.

docs.title: Conditioning
docs.text:
Physical conditioning supports your technique. Weak forearms, a stiff shoulder, or poor cardio will undermine even perfect form under pressure.

Page Focus Warm-Up Pre-training mobility and activation Strength & Power Grip, forearm, shoulder, and rotational power Recovery Cool-down, stretching, injury prevention

Conditioning is secondary to technique — until it isn't

For beginners: focus on technique. As you advance, physical limitations (grip endurance, shoulder mobility) will start to cap your growth. Address them proactively.

docs.title: Recovery & Injury Prevention
docs.text: Kali is hard on the wrists, elbows, and shoulders. Build recovery habits from day one.

docs.title: 1. Wrist Stretches (2 min)
docs.text:
• Extensor stretch: Arm extended, palm facing down. Use other hand to gently pull fingers downward. 30 sec per wrist.
  • Flexor stretch: Arm extended, palm facing up. Use other hand to gently pull fingers backward. 30 sec per wrist.

docs.title: 2. Forearm Cross-Friction Massage (2 min)
docs.text:
• Use thumb to apply firm cross-grain pressure along the forearm muscles
  • 1 minute per arm
  • Helps break up adhesions from high-volume striking

docs.title: 3. Shoulder Cross-Body Stretch (1 min)
docs.text:
• Pull one arm across your chest with the other
  • 30 sec per side

docs.title: 4. Thoracic Spine Rotation (2 min)
docs.text:
• Sit cross-legged, hands behind head
  • Rotate torso left and right slowly — 10 reps each direction

docs.title: 5. Hip Flexor Stretch (2 min)
docs.text:
• Low lunge position
  • Drop the back knee, push hips forward
  • 1 minute per side

docs.title: Common Injuries & Prevention
docs.text: Injury Why It Happens Prevention Wrist tendinitis High volume striking without warm-up Never skip wrist warm-up; wrist roller conditioning Tennis elbow (lateral epicondylitis) Overuse, poor grip mechanics Check grip pressure; forearm strengthening Shoulder impingement Overhead striking without mobility Face pulls, shoulder mobility work Bruised forearms Normal from partner drills Train with proper gear; accept it as part of Kali

docs.title: Sleep & Nutrition
docs.text:
No stretching routine compensates for bad sleep or nutrition.

  • Sleep: 7–9 hours. Skill consolidation and tissue repair both happen overnight.
  • Protein: ~1.6g per kg bodyweight daily supports muscle repair from high-volume training.
  • Hydration: Dehydrated muscle is stiffer and more injury-prone.

When to stop training and see a doctor

  • Sharp joint pain (not muscle soreness) during or after training
  • Numbness or tingling in the hands or fingers (nerve involvement)
  • Pain that persists more than 3 days after training
  • Any swelling that doesn't resolve with 24 hours of rest + ice

DOMS (delayed onset muscle soreness) is normal. Sharp joint pain is not. Know the difference.

docs.title: Strength & Power Training
docs.text: Kali-specific strength needs: grip endurance, forearm conditioning, rotational core power, and shoulder stability.

docs.title: Rice Bucket Training
docs.text:
Classic martial arts forearm conditioner. Fill a bucket with dry rice and plunge your hands in repeatedly.

  • Open-close grip: 3 × 30 seconds
  • Finger extension against resistance: 3 × 30 seconds
  • Wrist rotation in the rice: 3 × 30 seconds

Why: Builds grip endurance specific to stick work — not just raw squeeze strength.

docs.title: Stick Wrist Roller
docs.text:
Tie a weight (0.5–2 kg) to a short dowel with a cord. Roll the weight up by rotating the wrists alternately.

  • 3 sets wrist-up (palms down)
  • 3 sets wrist-down (palms up)
  • Add weight as the exercise becomes easy

docs.title: Stick Rotations
docs.text:
Hold a stick at arm's length, parallel to the floor. Rotate the wrist to point the tip in circles.

  • 20 inward, 20 outward — per hand
  • Progress to a weighted stick

docs.title: Rotational Power (Core)
docs.text: Kali strikes get their power from hip and core rotation, not arm strength. Train this directly.

docs.title: Medicine Ball Rotational Throw
docs.text:
• Stand sideways to a wall (or with a partner)
  • Hold a 4–6 kg medicine ball at waist height
  • Rotate hips and throw the ball against the wall explosively
  • Catch the rebound and repeat
  • 3 × 10 per side

docs.title: Pallof Press
docs.text:
Anti-rotation core exercise — builds the stability to anchor your rotation.

  • Attach a resistance band to a fixed point at chest height
  • Stand sideways, hold the band at your chest
  • Press it straight out, hold 2 seconds, return
  • 3 × 12 per side

docs.title: Band Pull-Aparts
docs.text:
• Hold a resistance band at chest height, arms extended
  • Pull the band apart until it touches your chest
  • Slow and controlled — 3 × 20

docs.title: Face Pulls
docs.text:
• Resistance band or cable at face height
  • Pull toward your face, elbows high and wide
  • 3 × 15 — important for shoulder health with high-volume striking

docs.title: Single-Arm Bottoms-Up Kettlebell Press
docs.text: Challenges shoulder stability in an unstable grip — mimics the reactive grip of stick work.

docs.title: Weekly Schedule Suggestion
docs.text:
Day Focus Monday Technique (primary), grip work after Tuesday Rest or light conditioning Wednesday Technique + rotational power Thursday Rest Friday Technique + shoulder stability Saturday Sparring / partner drills Sunday Full rest or recovery

Conditioning should not exhaust you for technique sessions

If your conditioning work is leaving your forearms or shoulders too sore to train Kali properly — you've done too much. Conditioning serves the art, not the other way around.

docs.title: Warm-Up Routine
docs.text: Duration: 10–15 minutes Goal: Raise core temperature, mobilise the joints used in Kali, and activate the nervous system.

docs.title: 1. General Warm-Up (3 min)
docs.text:
• Light jogging / jumping jacks / skipping in place
  • Goal: break a light sweat, heart rate to ~120 BPM

docs.title: 2. Wrist Circles (1 min)
docs.text:
Kali places enormous stress on the wrists. Warm them up first.

  • Extend both arms forward, palms down
  • Make slow full circles — 10 inward, 10 outward
  • Progress to holding a stick and making the same circles

docs.title: 3. Shoulder Rolls & Arm Circles (1 min)
docs.text:
• 10 forward shoulder rolls, 10 backward
  • 10 small arm circles forward, 10 backward
  • 10 big arm circles forward, 10 backward

docs.title: 4. Hip Circles (30 sec)
docs.text:
• Hands on hips, feet shoulder-width
  • Large, slow circles at the hip — 10 each direction

docs.title: 5. Leg Swings (1 min)
docs.text:
• Hold a wall or partner for balance
  • 10 forward-backward leg swings per leg
  • 10 lateral leg swings per leg

docs.title: 6. Deep Lunge with Rotation (1 min)
docs.text:
• Step into a deep lunge
  • Twist torso toward the lead leg, reaching overhead arm to the sky
  • 5 per side, hold each for 3–4 seconds

docs.title: 7. Shadow Sinawali — Slow (3 min)
docs.text:
• Heaven Six in the air, no power
  • Focus on full range of motion — let the shoulders open
  • This transitions your brain from "normal mode" to "training mode"

docs.title: Quick Reference Card
docs.text:
# Exercise Duration 1 Light cardio 3 min 2 Wrist circles 1 min 3 Shoulder rolls + arm circles 1 min 4 Hip circles 30 sec 5 Leg swings 1 min 6 Deep lunge with rotation 1 min 7 Slow shadow sinawali 3 min

Never skip the wrist warm-up

Kali practitioners are at higher risk for wrist and forearm repetitive strain. Cold wrists + high-velocity striking = recipe for injury. 60 seconds of wrist circles takes 60 seconds.

docs.title: Drills
docs.text:
Drills are how technique becomes instinct. The goal is not to memorise sequences — it is to build automatic responses through repetition.

Drill Type Description Sinawali Solo + Partner Weaving patterns — rhythm and flow Sombrada Partner Strike-block-counter flow cycle Sparring Partner Live application with controlled contact

docs.title: General Drilling Principles
docs.text:
1. Slow before fast. If you can't do it slow, you can't do it fast correctly.
  2. Both sides. Every drill, both dominant and non-dominant.
  3. No zombie reps. Stay mentally present — if your mind wanders, stop and reset.
  4. Film occasionally. What you feel you're doing and what you're actually doing are often very different.

docs.title: Sinawali — Weaving Patterns
docs.text: Sinawali means "to weave" in Filipino. These are rhythmic, flowing double-stick (or empty-hand) patterns that build coordination, timing, ambidexterity, and flow.

docs.title: Heaven Six (Anim na Langit)
docs.text:
The most fundamental sinawali pattern. All others are variations of this.

Striking sequence (from your perspective):

Right-high → Left-high → Right-mid → Left-mid → Right-low → Left-low → (repeat)

Partner feeding pattern: Your partner mirrors — their Right-high meets your Right-high, and so on. You are simultaneously striking AND receiving at the same rhythm.

Solo PracticePartner Practice
  1. Stand in fighting stance
  2. Strike Heaven Six in the air × 3 minutes
  3. Count aloud: "Right, left, right, left..."
  4. Focus: equal power from both hands, consistent rhythm
  1. Stand 1 stick-length apart
  2. Begin slowly — establish the rhythm together
  3. Sticks meet at the midpoint between you — neither partner reaches into the other's space
  4. Gradually increase speed as synchrony develops
  5. Do NOT race — if one person speeds up, the pattern breaks

docs.title: Earth Six
docs.text:
The reverse of Heaven Six — starts low, moves high.

Right-low → Left-low → Right-mid → Left-mid → Right-high → Left-high → (repeat)

Use: Builds comfort striking from low to high angles.

docs.title: Redondo (Circular Sinawali)
docs.text:
Instead of linear strikes, each hand makes a small inward circle before striking.

  • The circle is generated by the wrist and forearm, not the shoulder
  • Creates a whipping, unpredictable strike path
  • Harder to read and intercept than straight sinawali

docs.title: Abaniko Sinawali (Fan Sinawali)
docs.text:
Uses the fanning wrist motion (abaniko) on each strike rather than a straight downward arc.

  • Compact, close-range pattern
  • Each strike "fans" outward then snaps back
  • Very fast once the wrist conditioning is built

docs.title: Training Tips
docs.text:
Find the zone

Sinawali has a meditative quality at speed — you stop thinking and just flow. That state is what you're training toward. Don't rush to get there; it comes with reps.

Don't let the off-hand drop

The most common sinawali error: the non-dominant hand droops below the ideal strike zone. Both hands stay active at all times.

docs.title: Progression Ladder
docs.text: Stage Focus Time 1 Solo Heaven Six, slow 1 week 2 Partner Heaven Six, slow 1–2 weeks 3 Partner Heaven Six, increase speed Ongoing 4 Introduce Earth Six After Heaven Six is automatic 5 Combine Heaven + Earth alternating After both are solid 6 Redondo solo Whenever 7 Redondo partner After Redondo solo is comfortable

docs.title: Sombrada — Umbrella Flow Drill
docs.text: Sombrada (from Spanish: shadow) is a partner flow drill where one person feeds a strike, the other blocks and counters, and the pattern continues in a cycle. It is the bridge between drilling and sparring.

docs.title: Basic Sombrada Cycle
docs.text:
A 3-count exchange:

Feeder:    Strike (Angle 1) → Block partner's counter → Strike (Angle 1) → ...
Receiver:  Block → Counter-strike (Angle 1) → Block feeder's strike → ...

Both partners are simultaneously attacking and defending, flowing continuously.

docs.title: Step-by-Step (First Learn)
docs.text:
Setup: Partner A = Feeder, Partner B = Receiver. Standing at stick distance.

  1. A throws Angle 1 (forehand diagonal, high)
  2. B executes roof block, redirecting A's stick outward
  3. B immediately counters with Angle 1
  4. A executes roof block, redirecting B's stick outward
  5. A immediately counters with Angle 1 → back to step 2

The drill loops. Neither partner stops to "reset."

docs.title: The Keys to Good Sombrada
docs.text: Principle What it means Flow No pausing between block and counter — block IS the beginning of your counter Consistent rhythm Like a metronome — don't speed up or slow down mid-drill Eye contact Watch your partner's shoulder/torso, not the stick Alive hand Non-weapon hand should be checking on every exchange

docs.title: Adding the Alive Hand Check
docs.text:
Once the basic flow is smooth, add:

  • As you block with your stick, your alive hand checks the attacker's weapon forearm simultaneously
  • This mirrors a real defensive application — checking prevents a second immediate attack

docs.title: Variations
docs.text:
Two-Count SombradaAngle Variation SombradaLargo Mano (Long Range) Sombrada

Faster, less complex: - Feeder strikes - Receiver parries AND counters in a single smooth motion (no distinct block-then-counter) - Feeder absorbs counter and immediately re-strikes

  • Start with Angle 1 basic
  • After 10 reps, Feeder switches to Angle 2 (backhand)
  • Receiver adjusts block to match
  • Progress to calling angles randomly
  • Both partners take one step back
  • Only tip-of-stick contact — no body checked
  • Emphasises footwork: you must step in to strike and step back to avoid the counter

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Fix Muscling through the block The block is a redirect, not a bash — use the stick to guide, not smash Counter comes too late Block and counter are one motion. Drill: freeze after every block and check your counter hand — is it already moving? Watching the stick Focus on torso/shoulders — the stick follows the body Same speed always Vary rhythm in training. Slow → pause → burst. Prepare for unpredictability.

docs.title: Sparring
docs.text: Sparring is where everything gets tested. The goal is not winning — it is learning under pressure.

docs.title: Protective Gear (Required)
docs.text:
Do not skip gear

Rattan at speed to an unprotected head can cause serious injury. Gear up, every time.

Gear Purpose Full face mask / fencing helmet Head, face, neck protection Padded gloves (Escrima gloves) Hand and knuckle protection Forearm guards Block incoming strikes on the forearm Cup / groin guard Low attacks happen in live sparring Knee pads (optional but recommended) Ground game / footwork falls

docs.title: Sparring Protocols
docs.text:
Slow Flow SparringTechnical SparringLive Sparring

Goal: Application, not competition. Both partners move at 30–40% speed.

Rules: - Light contact only — touches score, power doesn't - No head shots with full power — ever - If a hit lands cleanly, acknowledge it ("yes") and reset or continue - Stop and debrief interesting exchanges

Best for: Beginners and as a warm-up for all levels.

Goal: Apply a specific technique or drill concept.

Rules: - One person has an assigned technique (e.g. "must counter every attack with defang") - Other person attacks freely at moderate speed - Debrief after each round: did the technique work? Why/why not?

Goal: Realistic application with full protective gear.

Rules: - Contact is allowed but controlled - No strikes to the spine or back of the head - Referee or partner present - Stop on a clear submission or "stop" signal

docs.title: Mindset for Sparring
docs.text:
Get hit, learn from it

Every time you get hit in sparring, something was wrong: your guard, your footwork, your timing, your angle. Treat each hit as a data point.

The goal is information, not ego

Sparring with a better practitioner is a gift. Do not avoid it because you lose — that's exactly where the fastest learning happens.

docs.title: Post-Sparring Debrief (Do This Every Time)
docs.text:
After each sparring session, write down:

  1. What worked well?
  2. What kept getting through my guard?
  3. One specific thing to fix next session

Over months, this log becomes your most valuable training resource.

docs.title: Sparring Drill: One-Tool Sparring
docs.text:
Both partners are restricted to one technique only. Example:

  • Both can only use Angle 1 and Angle 2
  • Both can only thrust (Angle 5)
  • One can only strike, the other can only block and defang

Constraints force deeper exploration of a limited tool set.

docs.title: Pages in This Section
docs.text:
Page Focus Stances & Footwork Body positioning and movement principles Weapon Grips How to hold your weapon correctly 12 Angles of Attack The universal targeting system in Kali

Why fundamentals matter

In Kali, a practitioner who truly understands the 12 angles and can flow between stances confidently will be more dangerous than one who knows 50 techniques but has shaky foundations.

docs.title: Weapon Grips
docs.text: How you hold the weapon determines power, speed, control, and your ability to flow into the next movement. A bad grip will sabotage even a technically correct strike.

docs.title: Standard Grip (Abierta / Open Grip)
docs.text:
The most common grip for single stick work.

How to grip:

  1. Hold the stick in your dominant hand
  2. Position the butt of the stick flush with the heel of your palm — about 1–2 cm of stick protruding beyond your hand (the punyo)
  3. Wrap all four fingers firmly around the stick
  4. Thumb rests naturally on the side — do not wrap thumb over the top
  5. Grip pressure: firm but not death-grip tight (~70% squeeze)

The punyo (butt strike)

Letting the butt protrude slightly lets you use the punyo as a short-range weapon — a backward hammerfist with the butt end. It also prevents the stick from being stripped from your hand.

docs.title: Alive Hand (Live Hand / Kamay)
docs.text:
Your non-weapon hand is never passive in Kali. It is called the alive hand or live hand.

Roles of the alive hand:

  • Check — intercept or redirect the opponent's weapon hand
  • Trap — pin or immobilise the weapon arm
  • Strike — open-palm slap, hammer fist, elbow
  • Guard — shield the face or body

Key drill: Practice slow-motion sinawali paying attention to where your alive hand is at every moment. It should never just hang there.

docs.title: Punyo Grip
docs.text:
A variation where you choke up on the stick, holding it in the middle section, with the butt end prominent.

When to use: - Close range / grappling range - When you need more control than power

docs.title: Grip Pressure
docs.text:
Phase Pressure At rest / guard Light (40%) — stays loose and fast On impact Firm (90%) — locks on contact Follow-through Relaxes immediately back to light

Death grip

Squeezing the stick at 100% throughout a drill will exhaust your forearm within minutes and slow your strikes. Grip peaks only on impact.

docs.title: Grip Switching Drills
docs.text:
SoloWith wall target
  1. Hold stick in dominant hand, standard grip
  2. Toss the stick from one hand to the other using a wrist flick
  3. Catch in standard grip on the other hand
  4. 3 × 1 minute each direction
  1. Strike a wall pad with angle 1 (forehand diagonal)
  2. On retraction, switch hands
  3. Strike angle 2 (backhand diagonal) with opposite hand
  4. Builds ambidextrous grip confidence

docs.title: Stances & Footwork
docs.text: Good footwork is what keeps you alive. Your stance controls your balance, your range, your mobility, and your angles of attack.

docs.title: 1. Fighting Stance (Depensa)
docs.text:
The default ready position.

Setup: - Feet shoulder-width apart, dominant foot slightly back - Weight distributed 50/50 or slightly back (60% rear) - Knees slightly bent — never locked - Weapon hand forward at roughly chest height - Non-weapon hand guard up near the chin or cheek

Key points:

  • Keep your weight on the balls of your feet, never your heels
  • Shoulders relaxed — tension = slow
  • Chin slightly tucked

docs.title: 2. Forward Stance (Pasa Forward)
docs.text:
Used for driving power into a strike.

Setup: - Dominant foot forward - Weight shifted forward (60/40) - Hips square or slightly angled toward target

Use case: Thrusting attacks, closing distance aggressively.

docs.title: 3. Side Stance (Lado)
docs.text:
Minimises your body profile — useful in weapon defence.

Setup: - Body turned sideways to the opponent - Weapon-side leg forward - Non-weapon hand tucked behind

Key points:

  • Your side profile is a much smaller target than your front
  • Limits your attacking angles — use situationally

docs.title: Triangle Step (Triángulo)
docs.text:
The foundational movement pattern in Kali. You move to three points of an imaginary triangle to evade and reposition.

         [Point A]  ← Strike comes in
        /         \
  [Point B]    [Point C]
(Step outside)  (Step inside)
  • Step outside (Point B): move to the weapon side of the attacker
  • Step inside (Point C): move to the non-weapon side

Tip

Always move off the line of attack first. Never step straight back.

docs.title: Passing Step
docs.text:
A linear shuffle step used to quickly close or open distance.

  • Lead foot steps first in the direction of travel
  • Rear foot follows — do not cross your feet
  • Stay low; don't bob up and down

docs.title: Replacement Step (Hakbang Palit)
docs.text: Swap your lead and rear foot positions in a single motion. Used to shift your angle rapidly.

docs.title: Footwork Drills
docs.text:
SoloPartner
  1. Mark a triangle on the floor with tape (~shoulder-width sides)
  2. Start at any point
  3. Call out "outside" or "inside" and step accordingly
  4. 3 × 2 minutes, smooth and controlled
  5. Progress: add a stick strike on each step
  1. Partner throws a slow feed (angle 1 strike)
  2. You triangle-step to either side and counter
  3. Switch roles every 10 reps
  4. Progress: partner varies the angle each rep

Common mistakes

  • Crossing your feet — instantly kills your balance
  • Standing flat-footed — you'll be too slow to react
  • Leaning back to avoid a strike instead of moving your feet

docs.title: 12 Angles of Attack
docs.text:
Imagine a clock face standing vertically in front of you, with 12 at the top and 6 at the bottom. Every strike in Kali travels along one of these clock lines. Learn to see these lines and you can read — and predict — any attack.

Note

Numbering varies between systems. This follows the clock-face framework used in class. When in doubt, defer to your instructor's numbering.

docs.title: Angle 1 — Forehand Diagonal (1 to 7)
docs.text:
Strike travels from roughly 1 o'clock down to 7 o'clock — a downward diagonal from your right shoulder toward the opponent's lower left.

  • Target: Left temple, left collarbone, left shoulder
  • Hand: Dominant (forehand)
  • Motion: The elbow leads upward to the wind-up position near 1 o'clock, then the forearm drops and the wrist snaps through toward 7 o'clock
  • Key point: Power comes from hip rotation and wrist snap at contact — not a shoulder swing

docs.title: Angle 2 — Backhand Diagonal (11 to 5)
docs.text:
Strike travels from roughly 11 o'clock down to 5 o'clock — a downward diagonal from your left shoulder toward the opponent's lower right. Mirror of Angle 1.

  • Target: Right temple, right collarbone, right shoulder
  • Hand: Dominant (backhand)
  • Motion: Elbow draws back and up toward 11 o'clock, forearm drops through toward 5 o'clock with a wrist snap
  • Key point: The elbow must stay up — dropping it below shoulder level telegraphs the strike

docs.title: Angle 3 — Forehand Horizontal (9 to 3)
docs.text:
Strike travels horizontally from 9 o'clock to 3 o'clock — a straight cross from your left to your right at mid-body height.

  • Target: Left ribs, left hip, left knee (depending on height)
  • Hand: Dominant (forehand)
  • Motion: A lateral sweeping motion; keep the tip level throughout — do not let it drop or rise mid-arc

docs.title: Angle 4 — Backhand Horizontal (3 to 9)
docs.text:
Reverse of Angle 3. Strike travels from 3 o'clock to 9 o'clock.

  • Target: Right ribs, right hip
  • Hand: Dominant (backhand)
  • Motion: Mirror of Angle 3 — same flat horizontal plane, opposite direction

docs.title: Angle 5 — Thrust (12 to 6, straight in)
docs.text:
Not a clock sweep — a linear thrust driving the tip straight forward toward the target.

  • Target: Throat, solar plexus, face
  • Motion: Extend from the elbow and shoulder. Think of punching the tip forward, not pushing
  • Key point: Retraction is half the technique. A thrust that stalls leaves you overextended and open

Retract immediately

After any thrust, pull back sharply along the same line. Lingering is dangerous.

docs.title: Angle 6 — Forehand Upward Diagonal (7 to 1)
docs.text:
The reverse of Angle 1 — rising from lower left (7 o'clock) up toward upper right (1 o'clock).

  • Target: Groin, inner forearm, weapon hand (defanging)
  • Hand: Dominant (forehand, rising)
  • Motion: Strike rises from low right-to-left; the wrist snaps upward at contact

docs.title: Angle 7 — Backhand Upward Diagonal (5 to 11)
docs.text:
The reverse of Angle 2 — rising from lower right (5 o'clock) up toward upper left (11 o'clock).

  • Target: Groin, inner forearm, weapon hand
  • Hand: Dominant (backhand, rising)

docs.title: Angle 8 — Forehand Low Horizontal (9 to 3, low)
docs.text:
Same direction as Angle 3 but dropped to knee/shin height. The clock face is now read at the lower third.

  • Target: Left knee, left shin
  • Key point: Requires a slight body drop or squat — do not just tilt the stick downward while staying upright

docs.title: Angle 9 — Backhand Low Horizontal (3 to 9, low)
docs.text:
Mirror of Angle 8 at low level.

  • Target: Right knee, right shin

docs.title: Angle 10 — Downward Thrust (12 to 6, downward)
docs.text:
A stabbing motion driving straight downward — 12 o'clock to 6 o'clock — into a target below you.

  • Target: Top of the foot, downed opponent
  • Grip: Often switches to an icepick grip for this angle
  • Context: Close-range, grappling situations

docs.title: Angle 11 — Forehand Upper Diagonal (3 to 9, high)
docs.text:
A high forehand strike traveling from 3 o'clock upward to 9 o'clock — rising from the right side toward the upper left.

  • Target: Left jaw, left neck, left ear
  • Variation: Often executed as an upward abaniko (fanning wrist strike)

docs.title: Angle 12 — Crown (straight down, 12 to 6)
docs.text:
A direct overhead downward strike — 12 o'clock straight down to 6 o'clock — landing on the crown of the head.

  • Target: Top of the skull, back of the neck
  • Defence: Roof block or payong (umbrella) block

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Angle Clock Line Direction Primary Target 1 1 → 7 Forehand diagonal down Left temple / collarbone 2 11 → 5 Backhand diagonal down Right temple / collarbone 3 9 → 3 Forehand horizontal Left ribs / hip 4 3 → 9 Backhand horizontal Right ribs / hip 5 Straight in Thrust Throat / solar plexus 6 7 → 1 Forehand diagonal up Groin / weapon hand 7 5 → 11 Backhand diagonal up Groin / weapon hand 8 9 → 3 (low) Forehand horizontal low Left knee / shin 9 3 → 9 (low) Backhand horizontal low Right knee / shin 10 Straight down Downward thrust Top of foot 11 3 → 9 (high) Forehand upward diagonal Left jaw / neck 12 12 → 6 Overhead straight down Crown of head

docs.title: Drilling the Angles
docs.text:
Solo — AirSolo — Wall TargetPartner — Feeding

Strike each angle in sequence, 10 reps each. First pass: slow and deliberate, full body rotation. Second pass: full speed.

Label zones on a wall pad with clock positions. Call the angle to yourself before striking. Progress: have a partner call angles at random — react, don't anticipate.

Feeder throws each angle slowly. Receiver names the angle aloud before blocking. Builds the recognition-to-response chain before speed is introduced.

Angles 1 and 2 first

The forehand and backhand diagonals are the most common attacks you will face and throw. Get these two deeply ingrained before moving on.

Train both hands

Every angle, both hands. Your non-dominant side will lag — that is normal and will close with time.

docs.title: Resources

docs.title: Equipment
docs.text:
• Sticks: Rattan from any Filipino martial arts supplier — ~28 inches, 3/4 inch diameter
  • Training knife: Rubber or hardwood training daga
  • Gloves: Escrima-specific gloves (not boxing gloves — you need finger articulation)

docs.title: Glossary — Kali Terminology
docs.text: Terms drawn from Filipino (Tagalog / Cebuano), Spanish-influenced Visayan, and common English transliterations used in training.

docs.title: A
docs.text:
Abaniko — "Fan." A fanning wrist-driven strike, circular in path.

Aldabis — A diagonal upward strike.

Arnis — The national martial art of the Philippines. One of three names for the same art.

docs.title: B
docs.text:
Baston — "Stick." The primary training weapon.

Buno — Filipino wrestling / grappling component.

docs.title: D
docs.text:
Daga — "Knife" or dagger. Also refers to knife fighting techniques.

Defanging the snake — Targeting the weapon hand / forearm rather than the body. Neutralise the weapon first.

Depensa — "Defence." Refers to defensive stance and defensive techniques.

Doble Olisi — Double stick. Both hands hold weapons.

docs.title: E
docs.text: Eskrima / Escrima — Another name for the Filipino martial arts system. Derived from the Spanish esgrima (fencing).

docs.title: G
docs.text: Gunting — "Scissors." A defanging technique where you intercept and cut/strike the weapon arm.

docs.title: H
docs.text:
Hakbang — "Step." Refers to footwork patterns.

Hakbang Palit — "Replacement step." Switching lead foot position.

docs.title: K
docs.text:
Kali — The oldest name for the Filipino martial art. Used especially in systems with older lineage. Sometimes considered an acronym: KA (kamay/hands) + LI (likha/creativity).

Kamay — "Hand." Also refers to the alive hand.

docs.title: L
docs.text:
Largo Mano — "Long range." Attacking from the maximum range of the weapon (tip zone). Footwork-intensive.

Live hand / Alive hand — The non-weapon hand; always active in checking, trapping, or guarding.

docs.title: O
docs.text: Olisi — "Stick." Another term for baston.

docs.title: P
docs.text:
Palis-Palis — A passing deflection that redirects an incoming strike without meeting it directly.

Palyo — A thrust or stab.

Palusot — "To slip through." Techniques that pass inside or outside a weapon.

Payong — "Umbrella." The umbrella block — stick held overhead horizontally.

Pekiti — "To cut into small pieces." As in Pekiti Tirsia Kali, a major system.

Punyo — The butt end of a stick. Used as a short-range striking surface.

docs.title: R
docs.text: Redondo — "Round / circular." Circular wrist-driven striking motion.

docs.title: S
docs.text:
Sinawali — "To weave." Double-stick flowing patterns. Also used as a two-person drill format.

Sombrada — "Shadow / umbrella." A flowing partner drill — strike, block, counter.

docs.title: T
docs.text: Triángulo — "Triangle." The triangular footwork stepping pattern.

docs.title: W
docs.text: Witik — A flicking wrist-snap strike, similar to abaniko but typically shorter.

docs.title: Lineage & History
docs.text: Understanding where Kali comes from deepens your practice and respect for the art.

docs.title: Origins
docs.text:
Kali / Arnis / Eskrima is the indigenous martial art of the Philippine archipelago. Evidence of blade-based fighting arts in the Philippines predates Spanish colonisation (1565). Spanish soldiers noted that Filipino warriors were already skilled fighters when they arrived — their blade arts were already mature.

The three names — Kali, Arnis, Eskrima — refer to the same family of arts but carry regional and lineage-specific connotations:

  • Kali: Older, associated with Pekiti Tirsia and some Visayan systems
  • Arnis: Associated with Modern Arnis, Remy Presas lineage; the official national sport name
  • Eskrima: Common in Cebuano regions; popularised internationally alongside Kali

docs.title: Major Systems
docs.text: System Key Figure(s) Characteristics Modern Arnis Remy Presas Emphasises tapi-tapi (checking), accessible to beginners Pekiti Tirsia Kali Leo Tortal Gaje Jr. Blade-centric, triangular footwork, aggressive Inosanto Kali Dan Inosanto Eclectic, synthesises many Filipino arts; widely taught in the West Sayoc Kali Sayoc family Knife system, information-based training methodology Doce Pares Canete family One of the oldest codified Cebuano systems Lameco Eskrima Edgar Sulite Heavy on largo (long range); emphasis on footwork

docs.title: Kali in MMA
docs.text:
Kali footwork, defanging, and blade concepts have been incorporated by fighters such as:

  • B.J. Penn — known to have trained Kali
  • Anderson Silva — studied Filipino arts among other systems

Dan Inosanto (student of Bruce Lee) was instrumental in spreading Kali to the West, embedding it into what became Jeet Kune Do concepts training.

docs.title: Your Instructor's Lineage
docs.text:
Add your instructor's name, their teacher, and the system you are studying here. Knowing your lineage connects you to the tradition.

Your Name
   └── [Your Instructor]
          └── [Their teacher]
                 └── [System / Founding figure]

Why lineage matters

Martial arts knowledge was historically transmitted directly from teacher to student. Knowing your lineage tells you what you're learning, why certain things are emphasised, and who to seek out when you want to go deeper.

docs.title: Weapons
docs.text:
Kali is taught weapon-first. The movements, footwork, and principles you learn with a stick translate directly to blade, empty hand, and other weapons.

Page Weapon Notes Single Stick Olisi / Baston Primary weapon. Start here. Double Stick Doble Olisi Builds ambidexterity and sinawali patterns Knife (Daga) Daga Edge awareness, grip, close-range application

Equipment

For training, use rattan sticks (about 28 inches, 3/4 inch diameter is standard). Rattan is forgiving on impact, won't shatter, and is inexpensive. Upgrade to hardwood or aluminium only for forms/demonstrations.

docs.title: Double Stick — Doble Olisi
docs.text: Double stick training builds ambidexterity, independent hand coordination, and rhythm. The patterns you learn here are the basis of sinawali drills.

docs.title: Grip — Both Hands
docs.text:
Use standard grip in both hands. The non-dominant hand will feel awkward initially — this is expected and will pass.

Critical: Do not let the non-dominant hand become passive. Both hands are attacking weapons.

docs.title: Coordination Principle
docs.text:
Double stick movements fall into two categories:

Pattern Description Alternating Hands strike in sequence — left, right, left, right Simultaneous Both hands strike at the same moment (high/low, inside/outside)

Start with alternating patterns. Add simultaneous patterns after coordination is solid.

docs.title: Basic Double Stick Striking Pattern
docs.text:
Heaven Six (the foundation of all sinawali):

R-high → L-high → R-mid → L-mid → R-low → L-low
(repeat continuously)
  • Each strike is Angle 1 (forehand) on the corresponding side
  • Keep the off-hand ready — not dropping to your side
  • Head stays still; hands do the work

docs.title: Drills
docs.text:
SoloPartner (feeding)
  • Heaven Six × 3 minutes non-stop
  • Count rhythm aloud: "1-2, 1-2, 1-2"
  • If coordination breaks, slow down — do not muscle through
  • Partner holds up pads in the matching zones
  • You strike each in sequence
  • Partner varies the rhythm to keep you reactive

Brain before speed

Double stick is more coordination than conditioning. 5 minutes of slow, deliberate, correct double-stick work is worth more than 20 minutes of sloppy fast reps.

docs.title: Knife — Daga
docs.text:
Training knives only

All knife work is done with rubber or wooden training knives. Never train live blade techniques with a real knife until your instructor clears you for supervised practice.

docs.title: Why Train the Knife?
docs.text:
• Develops acute awareness of edge and tip at all times
  • Teaches you to respect the danger zone (the opponent's weapon hand)
  • Cross-trains beautifully with empty hand and stick

docs.title: Grip Types
docs.text:
Forward Grip (Filipino Grip)Reverse Grip (Icepick)
  • Blade extends from the thumb side of the fist
  • Edge facing outward (sabre-style)
  • Most versatile for slashing and thrusting
  • Blade extends downward from the pinky side
  • Strong for close-range downward stabs and hooking
  • Limited thrusting range — closer quarters weapon

docs.title: Edge Awareness Drill
docs.text:
Before any technique: with training knife in hand, identify the four danger zones you present to an opponent:

  1. Weapon hand / forearm
  2. Lead leg / thigh
  3. Centreline (stomach/chest)
  4. Face / neck

Now identify those same zones on your training partner. This is what Kali calls reading the opponent's weapons.

docs.title: Forehand Slash (Pluma)
docs.text:
• Similar motion to Angle 1 strike with stick
  • Cut with the edge, not the flat — rotation of the wrist at contact
  • Retract immediately — do not leave the arm extended

docs.title: Thrust (Saksak)
docs.text:
• Drive the tip straight into the target
  • Alive hand checks the opponent's weapon arm simultaneously
  • Short, sharp — not a push

docs.title: Angle 6 Upward Slash (Defang)
docs.text:
• Rising cut targeting the opponent's weapon forearm or wrist
  • The classic "defang the snake" application
  • Executed as a counter after stepping offline

docs.title: Partner Drill: Touch and Check
docs.text:
1. Both partners hold training knives
  2. Slow motion — try to touch your partner's weapon hand
  3. Partner checks (intercepts) the attempt with their alive hand
  4. Switch attacker/defender roles every 30 seconds
  5. No power, no speed — this is a sensitivity drill

The alive hand is your armour

In knife combat, your non-weapon hand should never be idle. It is always checking, trapping, or protecting. A dangling alive hand is an invitation to be defanged.

docs.title: Single Stick — Olisi / Baston
docs.text:
The single stick is the entry point of Kali. Everything you learn here maps to blade, empty hand, and all other weapons.

Standard training stick: Rattan, 28 inches, ~3/4 inch diameter

docs.title: Forehand Strike (Abaniko / Fan Strike)
docs.text:
A fanning, wrist-driven strike primarily targeting the temple, neck, or collarbone.

Execution: 1. Hold the stick in standard grip 2. Raise the weapon to roughly ear level (not behind the shoulder — stay tight) 3. Fan the wrist outward — the stick arcs like a pendulum 4. Point of contact: the last 4–6 inches of the stick (the tip section is fastest) 5. Retract immediately along the same arc or redirect to next angle

Tip

The power in an Abaniko comes from the wrist snap, not a full arm swing. A compact, snapping Abaniko is faster and harder to read than a big wind-up.

docs.title: Downward Strike (Angle 1 & 2)
docs.text: See 12 Angles of Attack for detailed mechanics.

docs.title: Punyo Strike
docs.text:
Using the butt end of the stick as the striking surface. A short, sharp close-range weapon.

When: After a forehand strike, instead of fully retracting, drive the punyo backward into the target (face, sternum, stomach).

Range: Very close — typically used in trapping or grappling range.

docs.title: Core Blocks / Parries
docs.text:
Roof BlockUmbrella Block (Payong)Inside BlockOutside Block
  • Stick held diagonally above the head, tip pointing forward-up
  • Intercepts downward strikes (Angle 1, 2, 12)
  • Weight low, knees bent — you are a structure, not just an arm block
  • Stick held overhead, nearly horizontal, palm facing out
  • Covers a wider arc than the roof block
  • Good against incoming Angle 1 with simultaneous step offline
  • Parry the attacking weapon inward (across your centreline)
  • Opens the opponent's outside line for a counter
  • Combine with a triangle step to the outside
  • Parry the attacking weapon outward (away from your centreline)
  • Opens the inside line
  • Aggressive counter follows immediately

docs.title: Combination 1: High-Low-Thrust
docs.text:
Step Action Angle 1 Forehand diagonal strike Angle 1 2 Backhand diagonal strike Angle 2 3 Thrust to centre Angle 5

Focus: Smooth retraction between strikes. Each strike should feel like a drop into the next.

docs.title: Combination 2: Temple-Rib-Temple
docs.text:
Step Action Angle 1 Forehand diagonal (high) Angle 1 2 Forehand horizontal (mid) Angle 3 3 Forehand diagonal (high) Angle 1

Focus: Power transfer through rotation. Do not reset stance between strikes.

docs.title: Drilling Solo
docs.text:
• Shadow striking — all 12 angles × 10 reps each
  • 3 × 2 min rounds: alternate Combination 1 and Combination 2
  • Slow-motion form check: record yourself once a week

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Fix Telegraphing with shoulder wind-up Start motion from the wrist and elbow Retracting too slowly Treat retraction as the next attack, not a rest Standing flat-footed while striking Step with every strike — connect footwork to weapon work Focusing only on dominant hand Train left hand daily, even if awkward
